topics.title: 1.1 Landscape Systems: Option A Coastal Landscapes

outcomes.text: Explain how a coastal landscape works as a system, with inputs, processes, outputs, energy and material flows, and sediment cells.
Explain how winds, waves, tides, geology and ocean currents influence coastal systems.
Identify the terrestrial, offshore and human sources that supply sediment to coasts, including beach nourishment.
Explain how weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition are driven by energy and material flows on coasts.
Explain the formation of erosional landforms: bays, headlands, cliffs, shore platforms, geos, blow holes, caves, arches, stacks and stumps.
Explain the formation of depositional landforms: beaches, spits, on-shore bars, tombolos and salt marshes.
Use a high-energy and a low-energy coastline case study to show physical factors shaping landforms and how they are linked.
Explain how a coastal landscape system changes over timescales from seconds to millennia, using case studies including one beyond the UK.
Explain how falling sea level creates emergent landforms such as raised beaches, marine terraces and abandoned cliffs, and how they are later modified.
Explain how rising sea level creates submergent landforms such as rias, fjords and shingle beaches, and how they are later modified.
Using a managed coast case study, explain the strategy, its effects on sediment and energy flows, landforms and the landscape.
Using a coast developed economically, explain unintended effects on sediment cells, landforms, and consequences like retreat or protection.
Apply coastal skills: observation, measurement and mapping, field data statistics, sediment budget and mass balance calculations.

topics.title: 1.1 Landscape Systems: Option B Glaciated Landscapes

outcomes.text: Explain how a glaciated landscape works as a system, with inputs, processes, outputs, energy flows and glacier mass balance.
Explain how climate, geology, latitude, altitude, relief and aspect influence glaciated landscapes and glacier movement.
Describe types of glacier and how they move: glacier ice formation, valley glaciers, ice sheets, warm and cold-based ice, basal sliding and internal deformation.
Explain how weathering, mass movement, glacial erosion, nivation, transport and deposition operate in glaciated landscapes.
Explain the formation of glacial erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, troughs, roche moutonnée and striations.
Explain the formation of glacial depositional landforms: moraines, erratics, drumlins and till sheets.
Use a valley glacier landscape and an ice sheet landscape to show physical factors, linked landforms and change over time, with one case beyond the UK.
Explain how post-glacial climate change formed glacio-fluvial landforms such as kames, eskers and outwash plains, and how they are modified.
Explain how periglacial landforms such as patterned ground and pingos result from climate change, and how they are modified.
Using a periglacial case study, explain how human activity such as resource extraction alters flows, landforms and landscape, for example thermokarst.
Using a glaciated case study, explain how human activity such as dam building alters flows, landforms and the valley landscape.
Apply glacial skills: observation, measurement and mapping, field data statistics, sediment budget and mass balance calculations.

topics.title: 1.1 Landscape Systems: Option C Dryland Landscapes

outcomes.text: Explain how a dryland landscape works as a system, with inputs, processes, outputs, energy flows and the aridity index.
Explain how climate, geology, latitude, altitude, relief, aspect and sediment availability influence dryland systems.
Describe polar drylands, mid- and low-latitude deserts and semi-arid environments.
Explain how weathering, mass movement, fluvial and aeolian erosion, transport and deposition operate in deserts.
Explain the formation of desert erosional landforms: wadis, canyons, pedestal rocks, ventifacts and desert pavements.
Explain the formation of desert depositional landforms: barchans, linear dunes, star dunes, alluvial fans and bajadas.
Use a mid-latitude and a low-latitude desert to show physical factors, linked landforms and change from seconds to millennia.
Explain how earlier pluvial periods formed dryland landforms such as inselbergs and pediments, and how they are modified.
Explain how earlier colder periods left frost-shattered debris, nivation hollows and solifluction deposits in drylands.
Using a dryland case study, explain how water supply problems change flows, landforms and landscape.
Using a dryland case study, explain how economic activity such as tourism changes flows, landforms and the landscape.
Apply dryland skills: observation, measurement and mapping, field data statistics, sediment budget and mass balance calculations.
Explain why water and carbon matter for life, and how they cycle between land, oceans and atmosphere in open and closed systems.
Describe the distribution and size of the major stores in the carbon and water systems.
Describe the main inputs and outputs of the water cycle.
Describe the main inputs and outputs of the carbon cycle.
Explain the processes and pathways of the water cycle, from evaporation and condensation to runoff and catchment hydrology.
Explain the processes of the carbon cycle, including photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion and sequestration.
Describe water and carbon cycles in a tropical rainforest, their flows and stores, from a single tree to the whole forest.
Explain physical factors affecting rainforest water and carbon flows and stores.
Explain how deforestation and farming change a rainforest drainage basin's water cycle and carbon, soil and nutrient stores.
Evaluate rainforest management strategies such as afforestation and improved agriculture.
Describe water and carbon cycles in the Arctic tundra, with flow rates and stores, and the physical factors affecting them.
Explain seasonal changes in tundra cycles.
Explain impacts of oil and gas development on tundra cycles and how they are managed.

subtopics.title: Change in the cycles over time

outcomes.text: Explain dynamic equilibrium in the cycles and the balance of stores and flows.
Explain how land use change, water extraction and fossil fuel burning alter stores and flows.
Explain positive and negative feedback loops within and between the water and carbon cycles.
Explain short-term (daily, seasonal) and long-term changes in the cycles.
Explain why research and monitoring of the global water and carbon cycles are carried out.
Explain how the two cycles are linked through oceans, atmosphere, cryosphere and vegetation.
Explain how human use of water and carbon resources and long-term climate change affect the cycles.
Evaluate global strategies to protect the carbon cycle, including afforestation, wetland restoration, carbon trading and agreements.
Evaluate global strategies to protect the water cycle, including forestry, water allocation and drainage basin planning.
Apply skills for cycles: climate graphs, simple mass balance, rates of flow, unit conversions and field data analysis.
Use case studies of two contrasting local places to describe the characteristics and past and present connections that shape their identity.
Explain how shifting flows of people, resources, money and ideas have shaped places over time.
Discuss the difficulty of defining place, and the difference between space and place.
Explain why people perceive places differently depending on identity such as age, gender, religion and role.
Explain how emotional attachment to place affects behaviour.
Explain how globalisation and time-space compression affect sense of place.
Compare informal representations of place, such as film, music, art and blogs, in different media.
Contrast formal and statistical representations, such as census data, with informal ones.
Explain social inequality and how indices such as housing, health and education measure it.
Explain why spatial patterns of social inequality vary within and between places.
Explain how globalisation drives structural economic change such as de-industrialisation.
Explain how structural and cyclical economic change affect social opportunity and inequality.
Explain how government spending or cuts reduce, reinforce or create social inequality.
Use two contrasting places to show evidence of inequality, influencing factors and effects on daily life.
Explain the role of players such as governments, multinationals or international institutions in driving economic change.
Using a country or region case study, describe the place before economic change, the change and role of players, and impacts on people and place.
Explain placemaking and how governments and organisations present places to attract investment and regeneration.
Explain how architects and planners design meaningful, authentic places.
Explain how local community groups shape the places they live in.
Explain why and how places rebrand through reimaging and regeneration using sport, art, heritage, retail, architecture or food.
Explain the roles of different players in placemaking and why some groups contest rebranding.
Using a rebranded place, evaluate why it rebranded, the strategies, players, changed perceptions and success.
Apply place skills: qualitative place representations, media impacts, geospatial and quantitative data on places.

topics.title: 2.2 Global Connections: 2.2.1 Global Systems Option A Trade

outcomes.text: Define merchandise, services and capital as components of trade, and describe spatial patterns of inter- and intra-regional trade.
Relate trade patterns to development using indices such as value of exports and Human Development Index.
Explain how trade can promote stability, growth and development through flows of people, money, ideas and technology.
Explain how trade can cause inequality, conflict and injustice for people and places.
Explain how technology, MNCs and outsourcing, trading blocs, south-south trade, services growth and labour mobility have increased trade complexity.
Using an emerging or developing country case study, describe its trade patterns, how they changed, its interdependence with partners and trade's impacts.
Using an advanced country case study, show how core economies shape the trade system to their benefit, with its opportunities and challenges.
Using a low-income developing country case study, show how peripheral economies have limited influence, limited market access, and their opportunities and challenges.

topics.title: 2.2 Global Connections: 2.2.2 Global Systems Option B Migration

outcomes.text: Describe current spatial patterns in the numbers, composition and direction of international migrant flows.
Relate migration patterns to development using indices such as remittances and Human Development Index.
Explain how migration can promote stability, growth and development through flows of people, money, ideas and technology.
Explain how migration can cause inequality, conflict and injustice for people and places.
Explain how globalisation, young and female migrants, south-south corridors, refugees, policy change and bilateral corridors have made migration more complex.
Using an emerging or developing country case study, describe immigration and emigration patterns, changes, interdependence and impacts.
Using an advanced country case study, show how it influences the migration system, with its migration policies, opportunities and challenges.
Using a low-income developing country case study, show its limited influence over migration, with opportunities like remittances and challenges like skills loss.

topics.title: 2.2 Global Connections: 2.2.3 Global Governance Option C Human Rights

outcomes.text: Explain what human rights are and why global variation in rights norms exists.
Explain norms, intervention and geopolitics as ideas that make human rights complex.
Describe spatial patterns of forced labour, maternal mortality and capital punishment, and the factors behind them.
Explain economic, political and social factors behind variations in gender inequality, including education, reproductive health and employment.
Using a country case study, explain gender inequality issues, consequences for society, and changing norms and strategies.
Explain how human rights violations can cause conflict, and result from it, and how geopolitical intervention responds.
Explain the role of flows of people, money, ideas and technology in geopolitical intervention.
Explain how institutions, treaties, laws and norms promote and protect human rights.
Using a conflict area case study, explain how the UN, a national government and an NGO cooperate and what this means for local communities.
Explain short-term and long-term consequences of global human rights governance for citizens and places.
Using a low-income developing country case study, evaluate a human rights issue, governance strategy, opportunities and challenges.

topics.title: 2.2 Global Connections: 2.2.4 Global Governance Option D Power and Borders

outcomes.text: Define state, nation, sovereignty and territorial integrity and explain their role in the world political map.
Explain norms, intervention and geopolitics as ideas that make sovereignty and territorial integrity complex.
Explain how political boundaries, TNCs, supranational institutions and ethnic dominance erode sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Using a country case study where sovereignty is challenged, explain the causes, challenges to government, and impacts on people and places.
Explain how challenges to sovereignty and territorial integrity, such as resource access, can cause conflict.
Explain how institutions, treaties, laws and norms regulate conflict and reproduce the system of nation-states.
Explain the role of flows of people, money, ideas and technology in geopolitical intervention.
Using a conflict area case study, explain the roles of the UN, a national government and an NGO and the consequences for local communities.
Explain short- and long-term consequences of governing sovereignty issues for citizens and places.
Explain short- and long-term consequences of governing territorial integrity issues for citizens and places.
Using a low-income developing country case study, evaluate the issue, governance strategy, opportunities and challenges.
Describe methods for reconstructing past climate: marine and lake sediments, ice cores, tree rings and fossils.
Describe greenhouse and icehouse Earth periods, including Antarctic glaciation, Quaternary glaciation and the Holocene.
Explain natural forcing of past climate change: plate tectonics, Milankovitch cycles, solar output and natural greenhouse gases.

subtopics.title: Climate change in the industrial era

outcomes.text: Describe evidence of warming since the late 19th century: temperatures, shrinking ice, sea level rise, water vapour, snow and sea ice loss.
Explain why anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions have risen and how their global balance has changed.
Explain how added greenhouse gases enhance the greenhouse effect and affect the global energy balance.
Compare an advanced and an emerging country's emissions contributions over time.
Explain how the global warming debate evolved and how governments and organisations shaped it.
Evaluate the role and bias of media and interest groups in shaping climate change's public image.
Explain how climate modelling uses the carbon cycle, feedbacks and emission scenarios to project temperatures and sea level.
Describe current and projected climate impacts on people and environment, and their vulnerability.
Evaluate mitigation strategies: energy efficiency, low-carbon fuels, carbon capture, forestry and geoengineering.
Explain adaptation strategies, including retreat, accommodate and protect, and what adapted places could look like.
Using two countries at different development stages, compare climate impacts and the challenges of mitigation and adaptation.
Evaluate the IPCC, the Kyoto Protocol, carbon trading and national policies in shaping the international response to climate change.
Classify diseases as infectious or not, communicable or not, and epidemic, endemic or pandemic.
Describe the global distribution of malaria, HIV, tuberculosis, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Explain disease diffusion using the Hägerstrand model, including phases and barriers.
Explain how temperature, rainfall, relief and water sources affect disease patterns and vectors.
Explain how seasonal variation and climate change affect outbreaks and the spread of emerging diseases.
Explain the conditions for zoonotic diseases to spread from animals to humans.
Using a country hit by a natural hazard, explain how the hazard, environmental and human factors affected a disease, its impacts and management.
Explain how rising living standards affect disease susceptibility and epidemiological transition.
Explain why poorer countries have more communicable disease and richer countries more noncommunicable disease.
Using a country case study, explain air pollution's effect on cancers and the solutions.

subtopics.title: Dealing with communicable and noncommunicable disease

outcomes.text: Using a communicable disease case study, explain causes, patterns, socio-economic impacts and the success of mitigation strategies.
Using a noncommunicable disease case study, explain causes, patterns, socio-economic impacts and the success of mitigation strategies.
Explain how international organisations such as the WHO predict, monitor and combat disease.
Describe a global outbreak such as H1N1 or SARS, including its spread and distribution.
Using one NGO case study, explain its role in a disease outbreak at national and local level.
Explain how physical barriers help or hinder disease mitigation and response.
Evaluate mitigation strategies against global pandemics such as HIV/AIDS: screening, treatment funding and education.
Explain how medicines from nature depend on habitats, soil and climate.
Using a medicinal plant case study, explain growing conditions, trade, importance and sustainable use.
Explain conservation issues from the trade in medicinal plants.
Using a pharmaceutical transnational case study, explain breakthroughs, patents, manufacturing and global distribution.
Evaluate global, national and grassroots strategies for disease eradication, including the role of women.
Describe the distribution, area and volume of the world's oceans.
Describe ocean basin relief: continental shelf and slope, abyssal plain, ridges, rifts, trenches and guyots.
Describe horizontal and vertical variations in salinity and temperature.
Describe global surface currents and circulation in the North Atlantic.
Explain how light, temperature and nutrients, varying with latitude and depth, influence ocean ecosystems.
Compare food chains, webs and biodiversity in inter-tidal and deep-water ecosystems.
Using a renewable biological resource case study such as krill or whale, explain its use, management, stakeholder influences and thresholds.
Evaluate the use and management of oil and gas, wave and tidal energy, and sea-bed minerals.
Explain oceans as global commons and the tragedy of the commons.
Describe ocean zones: territorial waters, contiguous zone, EEZ and high seas.
Explain resource management through UNCLOS and marine reserves.
Identify the major ocean pollutants and their sources, including fossil fuel carbon dioxide, plastics, heavy metals and nuclear waste.
Using an oil spill case study, explain impacts on environment, ecosystems, fishing and tourism, and management.
Explain how currents spread and concentrate pollution, using a plastic accumulation case study in an ocean gyre.
Explain how ocean acidification and warming deplete fish stocks and threaten coral ecosystems.
Explain causes of sea level rise from climate change.
Using an island community case study, explain threats, impacts and short- and long-term adaptations.
Explain how global warming affects sea ice, ice-cover feedback and irreversible thresholds.
Using the Arctic case study, explain geopolitical implications, impacts on indigenous peoples, new routes and minerals, and international management.
Describe principal shipping routes, the changing scale of shipping, and the direction and type of ocean trade.
Explain how countries use oceans to exert influence, using naval strongholds and a marine conflict zone.
Describe the distribution and management of 21st century piracy.
Explain the use of oceans as escape routes for migrants.
Define food security through food access, availability and use.
Describe current global food security trends using hunger statistics and the Global Food Security Index.
Explain how food security patterns are dynamic and vary between and within countries.
Describe the physical conditions needed to grow food: air, climate, soil and water.
Explain feeding the world as a system of growing, processing, transporting and disposing of waste.
Compare food production methods: intensive and extensive, subsistence and commercial.
Explain how globalisation changes the food industry through demand and tastes.
Evaluate issues of food industry globalisation: food miles, inequality, obesity and price crises.
Evaluate opportunities of food industry globalisation: innovation, short-term relief and consumer choice.
Explain physical factors affecting food security: geology, soil and growing season length.
Explain social, economic and political factors such as land ownership and land grabbing.
Explain Malthusian and Boserupian positions on food security.
Using a place case study, show how human and physical factors combine to cause food security issues.
Identify regions, countries and people whose food security is most at risk.
Explain how storage and distribution pinchpoints such as the Suez Canal threaten food security.
Explain the causes of desertification and how it raises food security risks.
Using a dryland case study, explain how ecosystem, climate, hydrology, population change, land grabbing and climate change affect food security.
Explain how extreme weather, water scarcity and tectonic hazards affect food production and distribution.
Using an indigenous farming technique in an extreme environment, explain conditions, production methods and threats to food security.
Explain environmental impacts of raising food output: irrigation and salinisation, deforestation, changing landscapes and agrochemical water pollution.
Using a case study, explain short- and long-term impacts of food production methods on one physical environment.
Explain health impacts of food shortages, surpluses and poor diet, and of chemicals and pesticides.
Using two places at different development levels, explain how poor food security affects people's lives.
Explain how trading policies, the WTO and appropriate aid can help ensure food security.
Explain the roles of agribusiness, TNCs, food retailers and fair trade organisations in the global food system.
Explain strategies from short-term relief to capacity building and long-term system redesign.
Evaluate the effectiveness and sustainability of large-scale technological and small-scale bottom-up food security techniques.
Using two contrasting places, evaluate strategies used to ensure or improve food security.
Explain continental drift and plate tectonics: Earth's structure, convection currents, sea-floor spreading, paleomagnetism, ancient glaciation and fossils.
Describe the global pattern of plates and the features and processes at divergent, convergent (all three types) and conservative boundaries.
Compare explosive eruptions at convergent boundaries, effusive eruptions at divergent boundaries and hot spot eruptions.
Describe volcano size and shape, including super-volcanoes, and the volcanic explosivity index.
Describe volcanic hazards: lava flows, pyroclastic flows, gases, tephra, ash, lahars, flooding and tsunamis.
Compare shallow- and deep-focus earthquakes and measures of magnitude and intensity.
Explain how earthquakes shape landforms such as escarpments and rift valleys.
Describe earthquake hazards: shaking, ground displacement, liquefaction, landslides, tsunamis and flooding.
Using two countries at contrasting development, explain why people live in tectonic zones and the impacts of volcanic eruptions.
Using two countries at contrasting development, explain why people live in tectonic zones and the impacts of earthquakes.
Using two contrasting countries, evaluate volcanic hazard management: mitigating the event, vulnerability and losses.
Using two contrasting countries, evaluate earthquake hazard management: land-use zoning, building design and insurance.
Explain how tectonic risk has changed over time, using the disaster risk equation and possible future strategies.
Explain the relationship between disaster and response using the Park model.
Explain what makes data geographical and the ethical and socio-political implications of collecting and representing it.
Use different types of geographical information: qualitative, quantitative, primary, secondary, digital, spatial and big data.
Collect, analyse and interpret information, and question data sources, errors and misuse.
Communicate and evaluate findings and write extended geographical argument.
Collect and use digital data with geospatial technologies such as phones and tablets.
Explain the benefits of presenting and analysing data in GIS.
Use interviews and a range of methods, and evaluate textual and visual sources.
Explain the opportunities and limitations of qualitative techniques such as coding and sampling.
Calculate and use mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range and standard deviation.
Use tests of association and significance such as Chi-squared, Spearman's rank, Mann-Whitney U and T-test.
Use lines of best fit and correlation, and understand measurement, error and sampling.
Define research questions and place them in a theoretical or comparative context using literature.
Observe and record in the field, and justify the timing, sampling and data collection approaches.
Show practical knowledge of field methods and use them to collect good-quality data.
Select and apply suitable quantitative or qualitative techniques to analyse and represent field data.
Critically examine field data for accuracy and representativeness and apply theory to field observations.
Write up results with varied presentation, and evaluate the fieldwork, including its ethical dimensions.
Write a coherent, evidence-based analysis answering a geographical question.
